The government has appointed former Liberal minister Philip Ruddock to review whether Australian law adequately protects the human right to religious freedom. His appointment by cabinet was announced as a way to defuse a contentious debate about religious exemptions in upcoming same-sex marriage legislation.

Treasurer Scott Morrison emphasised the review is “no substitute” for legislative amendments on religious freedom, indicating the issue will still require parliamentary attention. Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull framed the review as necessary in light of the yes vote on marriage equality and the expected legislation that will follow.

There is division within the Coalition over timing and scope: senior conservatives such as Peter Dutton and Mathias Cormann have suggested a stand-alone religious freedom bill could be considered next year, while others, including Morrison and Liberal senator David Fawcett, want religious protections addressed concurrently with the marriage bill.

Turnbull warned against hastily drafted, broadly worded rights legislation, saying reforms should be cautious because they risk unintended consequences and legal uncertainty. He described the review as a “timely expert stocktake” to guide any future legislative reforms.

Ruddock has been asked to deliver his report by 31 March, and Turnbull justified the choice on the basis of Ruddock’s prior experience, including his service as Australia’s special envoy for human rights.
